guideTitle: Best NAS Drives for Home Media (2026)
metaTitle: Best NAS Drives for Home Media
metaDescription: NAS drives for home media compared on bay count, included disks, streaming and transcoding ability, and network speed, so movies and photos stay in one place.
expertTake: The UGREEN DXP2800 is the best overall pick because it is a true two-bay media server that you populate with your own disks and expand later, and the Buffalo LinkStation 220 is the value pick for people who want disks included and a simple setup. Anyone who treats a NAS as their only copy of photos should plan a second backup and may be better served by a plain external drive and a cloud backup.
introParagraphs: A network attached storage box is a small computer with one or more disk bays that serves files, photos and video to every device on your network. For home media the questions are how many bays you need, whether the box can handle video transcoding and whether disks come included.

This guide focuses on home media use and is honest about the limits. We evaluated each model from published specifications and patterns in owner feedback, with attention to bay count, processor class, network speed and year-three disk and software reliability. A NAS with disk redundancy protects against one drive failing. It is not a backup, so a second copy somewhere else still matters.

products.name: UGREEN DXP2800 2-bay NAS home media server, diskless
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP2800 is a two-bay home media server sold without disks. The design approach is a compact box that runs a vendor operating system with media apps, file sharing and photo backup, and lets you choose the drives you want. For a home with a movie library and family photos, two bays is the sensible starting point.

Compared with the larger UGREEN DXP4800 GT, the DXP2800 is smaller and cheaper but has less room to grow. Compared with the Buffalo LinkStation units, it is more capable as a media server, but you must buy disks separately. It suits people who want to build a proper media server on a budget.

Ownership is about disks and backups. Choose NAS-rated drives, set up mirrored storage for protection and keep an offsite copy of what you cannot replace. Update the operating system on a schedule and keep the vents clear of dust. A second drive of the same size makes mirroring simple, and buying two different batches of disks reduces the chance that both fail at once.
products.bestFor: Households that want a flexible two-bay media server.
pros: Two bays suit mirrored storage for a media library
Diskless design lets you choose your own drives
Media server apps handle streaming to TVs and phones
Compact body fits on a shelf
cons: Vendor software is newer than the long-established rivals

products.name: UGREEN DXP4800 GT 4-bay NAS for media servers and creators
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP4800 GT is a four-bay NAS aimed at larger libraries and creators. The design approach gives you room for four disks, which allows more capacity or protection levels such as RAID 5. For a family with a growing video collection, extra bays mean you will not outgrow it quickly.

Compared with the DXP2800, the GT offers more bays and more capacity but costs more and takes more space. Compared with the Asustor, it is a bigger machine with newer branding. It suits households with a lot of video or those who want to add storage over time.

Ownership requires a plan for disks and backups. Buy NAS-rated drives, consider a protection level that fits your capacity and keep an offsite copy. A four-bay box draws more power and makes more noise, so place it where you will not mind the hum. Plan for a UPS or at least a surge protector too, since a power cut during a write is a common cause of array trouble.
products.bestFor: Large libraries and households that expect to grow.
pros: Four bays allow more capacity and protection options
Room to expand without replacing the box
Media server apps support streaming and sharing
Diskless design lets you choose your drives
cons: More expensive than a two-bay box
Draws more power and takes more space

products.name: Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 AS1202T 2-bay NAS for home users
products.description:
The Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 is a two-bay NAS aimed at home users who want photo backup and file sharing. The design approach is simple hardware with a mature operating system known for ease of use. It does not try to be a heavy media server, but it covers the essentials.

Compared with the UGREEN DXP2800, the Asustor has a longer software record but less media muscle. Compared with the Buffalo LinkStation 220, it is diskless, so you choose your own drives. It suits users who want a reliable, easy-to-use box for photos and files.

Ownership is about drives and updates. Choose NAS-rated drives, set up mirrored storage and apply operating system updates. Keep the box ventilated and back up important data elsewhere. Its app store is smaller than some rivals, but the core jobs of file sharing, backup and photo albums are handled cleanly.

products.name: Buffalo LinkStation 220 4TB 2-bay NAS with included drives
products.description:
The Buffalo LinkStation 220 is a two-bay NAS that ships with 4 TB of disks installed. The design approach is to make setup simple, so you plug it in, connect to the network and start copying files. For a first NAS, that simplicity is the main attraction.

Compared with the LinkStation 210, the 220 has two bays, so you can mirror drives for protection. Compared with the UGREEN DXP2800, it is less capable as a media server and has older hardware. It suits people who want a plug-and-play box for photos and files.

Ownership requires attention to protection and backups. Set the box to mirror mode if you want redundancy, keep firmware updated and keep an offsite copy. Disks are included but not easily upgraded, so plan for the capacity you need. Because the disks are fixed to the model, a failed drive means a warranty claim rather than a quick swap from a spare.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want a plug-and-play NAS.
pros: Drives are included, so setup is simple
Two bays allow mirrored protection
Established brand with a long NAS track record
Lower price than building your own
cons: Included disks are less flexible than a diskless box

products.name: Buffalo LinkStation 720 8TB 2-bay home office private cloud
products.description:
The Buffalo LinkStation 720 is a two-bay NAS with 8 TB included, pitched as a private cloud for a home office. The design approach adds remote access features and more capacity than the 220. It suits households with larger media libraries that still want a simple setup.

Compared with the LinkStation 220, the 720 has more capacity and a more capable platform, but it costs more. Compared with the UGREEN DXP2800, it is easier to set up but less flexible. It suits users who want remote access to files and a large pool of storage out of the box.

Ownership requires thought about protection and security. Use mirror mode if you want redundancy, keep firmware updated and use strong passwords for remote access. Keep an offsite copy of important data. Remote access means exposing a device to the internet, so turn on the maker's two-step sign-in and keep the firmware current.
products.bestFor: Home offices that want remote access and large included storage.
pros: 8 TB included gives plenty of room for media
Two bays allow mirrored protection
Private cloud features support remote access
Simple setup for non-technical users
cons: Costs more than the entry-level LinkStation
Less flexible than a diskless media server

products.name: Buffalo LinkStation 210 4TB 1-bay NAS with included drive
products.description:
The Buffalo LinkStation 210 is a single-bay NAS with a 4 TB drive included. The design approach is the simplest possible NAS: one drive, no redundancy and a basic interface. It is a low-cost way to share files and stream basic media around the house.

Compared with the LinkStation 220, the 210 has one bay and no protection against drive failure. Compared with the UGREEN DXP2800, it is far simpler and less capable. It suits users who want to try a NAS cheaply and already have a backup plan.

Ownership requires a backup plan. A single drive means a drive failure loses the data, so copy important files elsewhere. Keep firmware updated and avoid using it as your only copy. Treat it as a convenience copy, and use a second drive or a cloud service for anything irreplaceable.
products.bestFor: Cheap trials and secondary shared storage.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Two bays allow mirrored storage, which protects against one drive failing, while four bays allow more capacity and levels like RAID 5. A single bay offers no redundancy. The UGREEN DXP4800 GT offers four bays, the DXP2800 and Asustor offer two, and the LinkStation 210 offers one. Pick the bay count you can grow into, since you cannot add bays later. As a guide, two bays with mirrored disks suit most families, and four bays make sense only once a library passes what two large disks can hold.

Buffalo LinkStations ship with drives, which simplifies setup. Diskless boxes like the UGREEN and Asustor let you choose NAS-rated drives and capacity. Diskless costs more upfront but is more flexible. Included drives may be harder to upgrade.

Streaming to a TV on the same network usually needs little processing. Transcoding video for phones or remote viewing needs a stronger processor. Check whether the box supports hardware transcoding if you stream away from home. Older boxes like the LinkStation struggle with it. A device with a slower processor can still play a movie to a TV that supports the file format directly, which is called direct play and needs almost no processing.

A gigabit port tops out around 110 megabytes per second in practice. Faster ports, such as 2.5 gigabit, help only if your network supports them. For streaming movies, gigabit is plenty. Wi-Fi often becomes the bottleneck. Cheap switches and long thin cables can also cap speed, so check the whole path from the NAS to the TV rather than just the NAS.

Operating system quality decides how easy the box is to use. Mature systems like Asustor ADM are easy to learn, while newer systems add features. Check for photo backup, media server apps and remote access. Poor software makes good hardware frustrating.

Mirroring protects against one drive failing but not against deletion, malware or fire. Keep a second copy offsite or in the cloud. A NAS is a convenience, not a backup. Plan for both. The 3-2-1 rule is a good habit: three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one off site.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bays and growth
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared bay counts and what they allow. The UGREEN DXP4800 GT offers the most room, while the LinkStation 210 offers the least. We matched bay counts to typical library sizes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Media capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at processors and media apps. The UGREEN boxes lean toward media, while the Buffalo boxes lean toward file storage. Transcoding support was a key factor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and software
howWeEvaluated.description: We read owner feedback on setup and software quality. The LinkStations are simple, the Asustor is mature and the UGREEN is newer. Ease of use was weighted for non-technical buyers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Protection and backups
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered redundancy options and what owners say about reliability. Mirrored two-bay boxes beat single-bay units. We stressed that a NAS is not a backup.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value in context
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each box in the home range and asked what it gives up. The LinkStation 220 is the value pick, the DXP2800 is the best balance and the DXP4800 GT is the growth pick. Warranty terms were a tiebreaker.

faq.q: Do I need a NAS for home media?
faq.a: Not always. A USB drive on a router or a streaming box may be enough. A NAS helps if many devices share a library or you want photo backup and remote access. If you only watch downloaded movies on one TV, a USB drive may be the cheaper and simpler answer.

faq.q: How much should a home NAS cost?
faq.a: Prices move, so check the current listing. Single-bay units with a drive are cheapest, two-bay boxes cost more and four-bay media servers sit near the top. Remember to budget for drives if the box is diskless.

No. RAID protects against a drive failing but not against deletion, malware or fire. Keep a second copy offsite or in the cloud. A mirrored pair also copies mistakes instantly, so a deleted folder disappears from both drives at once.

faq.q: What drives should I buy for a NAS?
faq.a: Choose drives rated for NAS use, which are built for constant operation and vibration. Desktop drives may fail sooner in multi-bay boxes. Matching the capacity and speed of both drives in a pair keeps performance steady.

Some can, if the processor and software support it. Older boxes struggle. Check the specifications if you stream to phones or away from home. Remote playback also depends on your home upload speed, which is often much lower than your download speed.

faq.q: Can I use Wi-Fi with a NAS?
faq.a: The NAS itself should connect by Ethernet. Your devices can use Wi-Fi, but speeds will vary. For big transfers, use a wired connection.
